questions.q: What is an 'implementation vulnerability' in the sense used here?
choices: A flaw in how C/C++/Objective-C code is written that lets an attacker corrupt memory
A weakness in a system's high-level design
A logic bug where the code faithfully does the wrong thing
A misconfigured server or network device
questions.explain: Implementation flaws are mistakes in the written code (here, C-family code) that allow attacker-controlled memory corruption. Design issues and logic bugs are a different category.

questions.q: Which of these corrupts memory only indirectly?
choices: A stack buffer overflow
A heap buffer overflow
An integer overflow whose bad result later causes a stack or heap overflow
A strcpy() that writes past the end of a local array
questions.explain: Stack and heap overflows corrupt memory directly. Integer overflows and other integer issues corrupt it indirectly, because they lead to stack or heap overflows later.

questions.q: What does an attacker usually try to gain by exploiting memory corruption?
choices: Arbitrary code execution, giving full control of the system
Only a crash of the program
Credentials obtained by tricking a user
A copy of the victim's network traffic
questions.explain: Memory corruption is ultimately exploited to give the attacker full control of the system, typically through arbitrary code execution.

questions.q: Which of these attack types are NOT memory-corruption vulnerabilities that lead to arbitrary attacker code execution?
choices: Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS)
Social engineering
Eavesdropping
Cyber-physical attacks
A heap overflow that lets the attacker run their own code
questions.explain: DDoS, social engineering, web application attacks, eavesdropping and cyber-physical attacks are other attack families. A heap overflow leading to code execution is exactly the memory-corruption kind.

questions.q: If you can't see how a vulnerability could be exploited, it's reasonable to treat it as harmless.
questions.explain: It is often unclear whether a bug is exploitable. Attackers will jump through many hoops to exploit things that look hard, so 'that seems hard, nobody could exploit it' is not a safe conclusion.

questions.q: Understanding vulnerabilities is the shared starting point for two different paths: secure development and vulnerability exploitation.
questions.explain: The 'two roads' slide: knowing vulnerabilities leads either to secure development (avoiding them) or to vulnerability exploitation (using them).

questions.q: Vulnerabilities in code harm real people. Which of these harm a person INDIRECTLY?
choices: An attack on the company the person works for
An attack on their local, state, territorial or national government
An attack on critical infrastructure such as water treatment or the power grid
An attack on their personal computer
An attack on a company they own
questions.explain: Direct harm means attacks on a person's own computer or a company they own. Indirect harm comes through their employer (job losses), their government (lost tax revenue) or critical infrastructure.

questions.q: In the security industry, what is a 'script kiddie'?
choices: Someone who runs attack tools or scripts without really understanding how they work
A young but highly skilled exploit developer
An insider who backdoors their company's product
A government-sponsored hacking group
questions.explain: A script kiddie has gotten hold of attack tools and runs the scripts successfully without knowing how they work.

questions.q: The governments you might need to worry about as attackers include your own (domestic) government, not just foreign ones.
questions.explain: Possible attackers include governments, both foreign and domestic. Which ones matter depends on your position and your threats.

questions.q: A company can be the source of an attack even when backdooring someone isn't company policy, because a well-placed malicious insider can still do it.
questions.explain: Companies can be attackers (for example when compelled by a government, or through corporate espionage), and attacks can also come from malicious insiders.

questions.q: Why does an attack that steals money from a local government harm ordinary residents?
choices: The money is effectively tax revenue, so fewer roads get paved, fewer library books get bought, and so on
It doesn't; only the government's IT staff are affected
Residents' personal computers are automatically infected too
Insurance always covers the loss, so there is no harm
questions.explain: Money stolen from a government is stolen from tax revenue. Closer to local government, a loss of a few million dollars means fewer services.

questions.q: In Microsoft's data on systems software (2016 through 2019), which vulnerability class ranked #1?
choices: Heap out-of-bounds
Use after free
Type confusion
Uninitialized use
questions.explain: The top classes were #1 heap out-of-bounds, #2 use after free, #3 type confusion, #4 uninitialized use.

questions.q: Which ranking matches Microsoft's top vulnerability classes in systems software (2016-2019)?
choices: 1 heap out-of-bounds, 2 use after free, 3 type confusion, 4 uninitialized use
1 use after free, 2 heap out-of-bounds, 3 uninitialized use, 4 type confusion
1 stack corruption, 2 heap out-of-bounds, 3 use after free, 4 type confusion
1 type confusion, 2 uninitialized use, 3 heap out-of-bounds, 4 use after free
questions.explain: Heap out-of-bounds, then use after free, then type confusion, then uninitialized use.

questions.q: In Microsoft's 2006-2019 chart of memory-safety CVEs, which category shrank to almost nothing over time?
choices: Stack corruption
Heap corruption
Heap out-of-bounds read
Use after free
questions.explain: There were more stack overflows early on (31 in 2006), but stack corruption fell to almost nothing in later years.

questions.q: Microsoft's chart shows a big spike of use-after-free vulnerabilities in one patch year. Which year?
questions.explain: Around 2014 there was a large batch of use-after-free CVEs (184 that year).

questions.q: In Microsoft's data, both the total number of memory-safety CVEs per year and the mix of vulnerability types changed over time.
questions.explain: The yearly total grew (roughly 150 in 2006 versus several hundred in 2019), and the share of each type also changed from year to year.

questions.q: In Microsoft's chart, one CVE can be counted in more than one vulnerability category.
questions.explain: The chart notes that a CVE may have multiple root causes, so it can be counted in multiple categories.

questions.q: What does the lecture say about newer, more sophisticated attack types?
choices: They are often just ways to reopen and unlock the older kinds of attacks that attackers are more comfortable with
They have made the older vulnerability types irrelevant
They only affect languages other than C and C++
They can't be understood without first studying web application attacks
questions.explain: Newer attack types often aim to get back to the earlier, simpler kinds of exploitation. That is why the simpler vulnerability types are a foundation for the harder ones.

questions.q: What does the acronym ACID stand for?
questions.explain: ACID = Attacker-Controlled Input Data, a two-syllable stand-in for longer terms like 'attacker-controlled input' or 'tainted data'.

questions.q: Which of these are longer terms that ACID is meant to replace?
choices: Tainted data
Attacker-controlled input
Sanitized data
Trusted constants
questions.explain: 'Attacker-controlled input' and 'tainted data' mean the same thing as ACID. Sanitized data and trusted constants are the opposite.

questions.q: What is a developer's job with respect to ACID?
choices: Neutralize, sanitize, and otherwise stop the ACID from harming users
Use the ACID to take over target systems
Pass the ACID along unchanged so other functions can validate it
Log the ACID for later analysis but otherwise process it normally
questions.explain: Developers must neutralize, sanitize and otherwise stop ACID. Exploiters, on the other hand, use ACID to 'hack the planet'.

questions.q: ACID only endangers the function that first receives it.
questions.explain: ACID flows through programs and corrupts everything it comes into contact with, not just the entry point.

questions.q: What is the hex value of the ASCII character 'A', which is why 0x41414141 appears so often in exploit demos?
questions.explain: 'A' is 0x41, so a run of A's shows up as 0x41414141 in a register or memory dump, making it easy to spot where attacker-controlled input landed.
